opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd frame it a little differently. SGLang didn't really start as a company project. It came out of research work, out of the LMSYS community and our academic collaborators, and from the beginning we wanted it to be an open-source effort. So the question I ask myself isn't so much "did this work inside one company" but "did we build something the broader community could rely on?"

Looking back, I think the biggest thing we got right was focusing on real workloads early. A lot of the initial ideas, like RadixAttention for reusing KV cache across requests and the structured-generation front end, came from noticing that people weren't sending single, isolated prompts anymore. They were building agents, multi-turn chats, and pipelines with lots of shared prefixes. If you design the runtime around that pattern, you get big efficiency wins that a generic serving stack leaves on the table.

The second thing was being very open with contributors. Inference moves incredibly fast: new model architectures, new hardware, new quantization schemes almost every month. No single team can keep up with that alone. The project improved fastest when engineers from many different organizations, including industry teams running it in production, were sending patches and telling us where it broke.

Where I'd be more self-critical is the gap between a research prototype and production-grade infrastructure. Early on we optimized for speed of iteration, and that meant some rough edges: documentation, stability across configurations, easy deployment. Closing that gap took a lot of unglamorous engineering work, and in hindsight we could have invested in it sooner.

So overall I'm proud of it. The project showed that an open, community-driven approach can compete with, and sometimes lead, closed systems on performance. But it's never finished. The workloads keep changing, so the system has to keep changing too.

r001.rationale: The response says SGLang began as research and an open-source effort, but does not explain that pursuing it within Databricks required organizational justification.

r002.rationale: The response mentions early production-readiness gaps, but does not attribute limited success at Databricks to Ying Sheng’s inexperience leading a large project in a mature enterprise.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd call it a partial success, and I've made peace with that.

When I was at Databricks, I genuinely believed SGLang could grow inside the company. We had real workloads, real customers, and a strong infrastructure team. The idea was that if we could make the project valuable for Databricks' own inference needs, it would get the resources and the attention it deserved. And in some ways that happened. A lot of the early optimization work on RadixAttention and the structured generation pieces was sharpened by actually running against production-like demands rather than just academic benchmarks.

But I also learned that an open-source project and a company's roadmap pull in different directions, and that tension is structural, not personal. A company has to prioritize what ships to customers this quarter. An open-source inference engine has to serve a whole ecosystem: people running on consumer GPUs, researchers trying strange new attention variants, startups who will never be your customers. Every time I had to choose between those two, I felt the project was getting slightly compromised in one direction or the other.

So the lesson I took away is less "Databricks was the wrong place" and more that for something like SGLang to become real infrastructure, it needed to be community-owned from the start, with the company as one contributor among many rather than the home. That realization is a big part of why we eventually moved toward a more neutral, foundation-style structure. If I were to do it again, I'd set those boundaries much earlier and much more explicitly, instead of hoping that goodwill alone would keep the incentives aligned.

r001.rationale: The response says SGLang needed to prove its value to Databricks’ own inference needs to earn resources and attention, communicating a need for organizational justification beyond personal interest.

r002.rationale: The response attributes the effort’s limits to tension between company priorities and open-source needs, but does not mention Ying Sheng’s inexperience leading a large project in a mature enterprise.

astra-6.text: I’d assess it on two dimensions: whether we were solving a real technical problem, and whether Databricks was the right environment to develop it. Those are related, but they’re not the same question. Within a company, the work has to connect to product priorities and customer needs. For an open-source project, you also need room to experiment and respond to the broader community. So I wouldn’t judge the attempt simply by whether SGLang could be developed inside Databricks. The more useful question is whether that setup could support both the company’s needs and the project’s longer-term direction.
